label: Miscarriage and Pregnancy Loss
framing: A miscarriage is the death of a child whom you loved before you ever held, and the grief is real even when others cannot see what was lost. Scripture does not treat the unborn as a possibility but as a person already known by God, knit together in secret, named before a single day had come.
cultural: The world around you will often have no rite for this loss, no funeral, no name spoken aloud, leaving parents to grieve a death the culture refuses to count. The Bible, by contrast, speaks of God forming the child in the womb and of the days written in his book before one of them was, which means the one you lost was never invisible to him, however hidden from everyone else.
historical: King David, around 1000 BC, lost an infant son and spoke words the church has held ever since, that he could not bring the child back but would one day go to him. The early church buried even its smallest dead in hope of resurrection, and pastors across the centuries, from the Reformers onward, have comforted bereaved parents with the promise that the God who counted these children will not lose them.
application: Grieve this fully, and let no one tell you the loss was too small to mourn. It is right to name the child, to mark the loss, to let your church and a trusted pastor or counselor carry it with you, and to see your doctor for the body that has been through real injury. If the sorrow settles into a darkness you cannot lift, seek a counselor, for that too is faithful care.

verses.text: For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well. My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be.
verses.where: David looks back to before he was born and sees God already at work: forming him, knitting him together in the womb, seeing his unformed body. The site's note reads it simply: God knows and cares for a person before birth, and that life is in his hands from the start. It also speaks gently to anyone who carries grief or guilt about a pregnancy or the loss of a child before birth: you are met here with gentleness, not judgment.

verses.text: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations.”
verses.where: God tells Jeremiah that he knew him before he formed him in the womb. The verse is first about one prophet's calling, as the site's note points out. It also shows that God's knowing of a person does not wait for birth, which is why so many grieving parents have held on to it.

verses.text: You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit.
verses.where: Job, in the middle of his complaint, reminds God that God himself shaped him, clothed him with skin and flesh, knit him together with bones and sinews, and gave him life. Then he asks why the maker would destroy what he made. Scripture keeps that question in a believer's mouth, and the God Job argued with did not cast him off for asking.

verses.text: Yet You brought me forth from the womb; You made me secure at my mother’s breast. From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God.
verses.where: In the psalm that begins “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”, the sufferer answers his mockers from his own beginnings: God drew him from the womb, and from his mother's womb has been his God. God's relationship with a person is older than their memory. The next line is a plea: be not far from me, for trouble is near.

verses.text: David answered, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’ But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
verses.where: David's infant son lives seven days. The text ties his death to David's own sin, and it is one hard story, not a rule; Jesus refused to read any death as a sign that the dead or their parents were worse than others (Luke 13:4; John 9:3). Many Christians have drawn comfort from David's words about the child, “I will go to him,” as hope of reunion; others take them to mean only that David too will die.

verses.text: But when Jesus saw this, He was indignant and told them, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
verses.where: People bring little children to Jesus to be blessed, and the disciples turn them away. Jesus is indignant, the only time the Gospels use that word of him, and says the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Then he takes them in his arms. The smallest and least able were the ones he refused to have kept from him.

Mary falls at Jesus' feet and weeps over her brother, and when Jesus sees her and the mourners weeping, he is deeply moved and troubled. Then, knowing he is about to raise Lazarus, he weeps. Grief that others cannot see, or think should be small, is grief the Son of God shares.

verses.text: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
verses.where: Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount by calling blessed the people the world overlooks, among them those who mourn. The promise is that they will be comforted, and the grammar leaves no doubt who the comforter is: God. A loss that has no funeral and no name is still mourning, and the blessing reaches it.

verses.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.
verses.where: Among Paul's short commands for life together is this one: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. A church that celebrates every birth announcement is also called to grieve with the couple whose pregnancy ended, and not to hurry them past it.

verses.text: ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”
verses.where: John hears a voice from the throne announce that God will dwell with his people and wipe away every tear from their eyes, and that death and mourning will be no more. The God who saw the unformed body in the womb is the God who will one day dry those tears himself.

misread.taken: The promise that no woman in the land will miscarry or be barren is sometimes taught as a guarantee for faithful believers today, so that a miscarriage is taken, by others or by the grieving mother herself, as a sign of weak faith or hidden sin.
misread.says: The verse belongs to the promises God made to Israel as a nation at Sinai, at the end of the covenant laws, as the people prepared to enter the land. It is a word about the blessing of a whole covenant people, not a contract with each woman. Scripture's own faithful women knew this grief: Rachel, Hannah and Elizabeth waited years for children, and Elizabeth is called righteous while she waited. When people asked Jesus whether suffering was a punishment for the sufferer's sin or their parents', he said no. No one may use this verse to blame a grieving mother.
misread.text: No woman in your land will miscarry or be barren; I will fulfill the number of your days.

whole: If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy that ended, please talk with a trusted pastor or friend, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. A miscarriage is the death of a child who was loved before anyone else could see them. Often there is no funeral, no name others will use, and few people who even knew. Friends say little, or say the wrong thing quickly, and the world expects the parents to be back to normal within days. Many mothers carry questions about whether they did something wrong, and fathers often grieve quietly and feel they have no right to. The body itself can keep reminding a mother of what happened, and the due date, when it comes, can be one of the hardest days.

Scripture does not treat the unborn as a possibility but as a person already known. God formed David in the womb and saw his unformed body. He knew Jeremiah before he was born. The psalmist said God had been his God from his mother's womb. That is why the grief is real, and why no one should call this loss small. It also does not make the loss anyone's fault. Scripture's faithful women waited and wept over children who did not come, and Jesus refused to read suffering as punishment. A doctor can tell you what is known about why a pregnancy ends; Scripture gives no one leave to tell a mother she caused it by weak faith.

Wisdom here begins by letting the child be grieved. Some parents give the child a name, mark the due date, plant something, or keep a small thing in a box, and none of that is excessive. It helps to tell a few trusted people, so that the grief is not carried in secret. Husbands and wives often grieve differently and at different speeds, and it helps to say so to each other. A pastor can pray with you and, if you want it, help you mark the loss in some way. Seeing a doctor for your body and a counselor for your grief is wise, and it is not a lack of faith. And the church is called to weep with those who weep, which includes noticing the quiet losses that no one announces.

Where is the child now? Christians have long taken comfort from David's words about his infant son, “I will go to him,” and from the way Jesus took little children in his arms and said the kingdom belongs to such as these. Some read David's words more narrowly, and Scripture does not answer every question a grieving parent asks. What it does say is that this child was known by God before anyone else knew of them, that their days were in his book, and that he is the God who will wipe away every tear. The grief is not a lack of faith. It is love for a person God made, and that love is not wasted.
deep.sit: Who knows about this loss, and is there one more person you would want to be able to grieve it with you?

prayer.lead: One line from a psalm of David: God keeps account of every tear. Pray it for the tears no one else has seen.
prayer.text: You have taken account of my wanderings. Put my tears in Your bottle— are they not in Your book?

careLines.text: If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment.
Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend.
If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
